blog.content.how-to-choose-a-clinic-sing: How to Choose the Right Clinic in Singapore: 7 Things to Consider
How to Choose the Right Clinic in Singapore | ClynicQ
Looking for a clinic in Singapore? Learn what to check before choosing a GP, physiotherapy, TCM or chiropractic clinic.
From choosing the right type of care to checking clinic credentials, costs and appointment options, here's what to consider before your next visit.
Mother and daughter at home looking up clinic options on a mobile phone
Finding the right care shouldn't be complicated.
When you're feeling unwell, dealing with an injury or looking for ongoing treatment, choosing a clinic isn't always as simple as picking the nearest one.
Singapore has many healthcare options, from general practitioner (GP) clinics to physiotherapy, traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) and chiropractic services.
So how do you decide which clinic is right for you?
Here are seven things worth considering before your next visit.
1. Choose the Right Type of Care
Not every clinic provides the same services.
GP clinics
A starting point for common illnesses, general medical consultations and preventive healthcare.
Physiotherapy clinics
Help assess and manage movement difficulties, injuries and rehabilitation needs.
TCM clinics
Provide traditional Chinese medicine consultations and treatments within their professional scope.
Chiropractic clinics
Focus on musculoskeletal care, although the suitability of treatment depends on your condition.
Not sure which service is appropriate? A GP can help assess your symptoms and advise whether further evaluation or referral is needed.
2. Location Matters, but Convenience Goes Beyond Distance
Searching for a "clinic near me" is often the first step.
A clinic near your home or workplace can make follow-up visits easier, particularly when you require multiple treatment sessions.
But distance isn't everything.
Consider the clinic's operating hours, appointment availability and how easy it is to plan your visit.
A clinic that's slightly further away but fits your schedule may be more convenient than one that's nearby but difficult to visit.
3. Check the Clinic's Credentials
Your health deserves proper care.
Before visiting a healthcare provider, check whether the clinic and practitioner hold the relevant licences or professional registrations, where required.
In Singapore, you can refer to official healthcare directories to verify applicable healthcare service licences and professional registrations.
Don't rely entirely on social media advertisements, testimonials or promotional claims when making healthcare decisions.
4. Understand the Costs Before Your Visit
Medical and therapy fees can vary between clinics.
Before making an appointment, consider asking:
What is the consultation fee?
Are medications, procedures or treatments charged separately?
Will follow-up sessions cost the same?
Are any applicable subsidies, insurance arrangements or corporate benefits accepted?
For eligible patients, certain GP and dental clinics participate in the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS). You can check participating clinics through the official CHAS clinic locator.
Understanding the expected costs upfront helps you make a more informed choice.
5. Check Whether the Clinic Accepts Walk-Ins or Appointments
Not all clinics operate the same way.
Some GP clinics accept walk-in patients, while many physiotherapy and other therapy providers operate primarily through scheduled appointments.
Before heading down, find out how the clinic manages patient visits.
For walk-in clinics, you may want to check whether remote queue joining is available.
For appointment-based clinics, check whether advance booking is required and how appointment changes are handled.
A little planning can make your visit more convenient.
6. Look Beyond Online Reviews
Reviews can provide useful insights into other patients' experiences, but they shouldn't be the only factor in your decision.
Pay attention to whether the clinic communicates clearly, explains its services and provides information relevant to your needs.
A good patient experience isn't just about friendly service. It's also about understanding your care options, knowing what to expect and being able to make informed decisions.
7. Make Your Clinic Visit Easier with Digital Tools
Choosing the right clinic is one part of the experience. Planning your visit is another.
Digital healthcare tools can help patients access clinic information and, depending on the clinic, manage certain aspects of their visit.
ClynicQ is a digital platform that connects patients with participating clinics and supports clinic-specific queueing or appointment workflows.
Whether you're visiting a GP or an appointment-based healthcare provider, check what options are available at your chosen clinic.
The goal is simple: make it easier to plan your clinic visit, with less uncertainty about the process.
Conclusion: Your Healthcare Journey, Your Choice
The right clinic isn't necessarily the closest, cheapest or most popular one.
It's the one that offers appropriate care for your needs, with qualified providers, clear information and a visit arrangement that works for you.
Take a little time to compare your options, ask questions and choose a provider you're comfortable with.
Looking for a more convenient way to plan your clinic visit?

blog.content.walk-in-clinics-singapore.t: Walk-In Clinics in Singapore: What to Know Before You Visit
blog.content.walk-in-clinics-singapore.s: Walk-In Clinics in Singapore: What to Know | ClynicQ
blog.content.walk-in-clinics-singapore.m: Looking for a walk-in clinic in Singapore? Learn about clinic hours, waiting times, queue arrangements and ways to plan your visit.
blog.content.walk-in-clinics-singapore.e: Looking for a walk-in clinic? Learn what to check before heading down, how clinic queues work and how to plan your visit.
blog.content.walk-in-clinics-singapore.i: Glass storefront of a medical clinic with an OPEN sign and the clinic's heart logo etched on the door
Feeling unwell and thinking of visiting a clinic?
Sometimes, making an appointment isn't practical. You might wake up with a fever, develop a sudden cough or simply need to see a doctor without planning days ahead.
That's where walk-in clinics come in.
But before heading down, it's worth understanding how walk-in visits work, what to check and how you can make your visit more convenient.
blog.content.walk-in-clinics-singapore.s: 1. Can You Visit a Clinic Without an Appointment?
Yes. Many general practitioner (GP) clinics in Singapore accept walk-in patients.
This means you can visit during their operating hours without booking an appointment in advance.
However, walk-in arrangements vary between clinics. Some may stop accepting registrations before closing time or limit walk-ins when demand is high.
Other healthcare providers, including physiotherapy, TCM and chiropractic clinics, may operate primarily through appointments.
Tip: Check the clinic's current operating hours and registration arrangements before travelling.
2. How to Find a Walk-In Clinic Near You
When searching for a clinic, convenience is often a priority.
You might start with searches such as:
Walk-in clinic near me
GP clinic near me
Walk-in clinic Singapore
Clinic open today
But the nearest clinic isn't necessarily the most suitable one.
Consider the type of care you need, the clinic's location, operating hours and whether it accepts walk-in patients.
You can also check official healthcare directories and clinic websites for relevant information.
For potentially serious or life-threatening symptoms, seek emergency medical care rather than waiting for a routine clinic consultation.
3. What Should You Check Before Heading Down?
A little preparation can save you an unnecessary trip.
Here are a few things worth checking:
Operating hours
Some clinics operate in separate morning, afternoon and evening sessions. Registration cut-off times may differ from published closing times.
Walk-in availability
A clinic may accept walk-ins generally but have different arrangements on certain days.
Consultation fees
Check whether consultation fees, medications and other services are charged separately.
Subsidies and insurance
If applicable, check whether the clinic participates in CHAS or accepts your insurance or corporate healthcare arrangements.
Queue arrangements
Find out whether you need to register physically at the clinic or whether remote queue joining is available.
4. Why Do Clinic Waiting Times Vary?
Even at the same clinic, waiting times can differ from day to day.
Factors may include:
The number of patients ahead of you
Consultation duration
Patients requiring additional attention
Staffing and clinic operations
Appointment and walk-in arrangements
A shorter queue doesn't always guarantee a shorter wait, as consultation times can vary.
If queue information is available, it may help you make a more informed decision about when to visit.
5. Can You Join a Clinic Queue Without Being There?
At participating clinics, remote queueing may allow patients to join a queue before arriving.
Instead of heading straight to the clinic just to obtain a queue number, you may be able to register remotely using a supported digital platform.
Depending on the clinic's system, you may also be able to view queue information before making your way down.
However, remote queue joining does not guarantee an immediate consultation or an exact waiting time.
Always follow the clinic's registration and arrival instructions.
6. How ClynicQ Can Help You Plan Your Clinic Visit
ClynicQ is a digital healthcare platform that connects patients with participating clinics.
For clinics that support remote queueing, ClynicQ allows patients to join the queue digitally and access available queue information.
ClynicQ also supports appointment-based clinic workflows, recognising that not every healthcare provider operates on a walk-in basis.
Whether you're visiting a GP or an appointment-based provider, the available options depend on the participating clinic.
The idea is simple: less uncertainty when planning your clinic visit.
7. Walk-In or Appointment: Which Is Better?
Neither arrangement is automatically better.
Walk-in visits can be useful when you need a routine consultation without a prior booking, subject to clinic availability.
Appointments may be more suitable for planned consultations, follow-up treatments or services that require dedicated time.
What matters is choosing appropriate care and understanding the clinic's visit arrangements.

blog.content.tcm-singapore-first-visit.e: Thinking of trying TCM? Learn what happens at a first consultation, which treatments may be offered, how to check practitioner registration and what to consider before your visit.
blog.content.tcm-singapore-first-visit.i: Storefront of BE TCM Clinic with its logo and signboard on the wall, and the glass door lettered with physician Khor Tze Hsin's MOH-registered TCM credentials
Thinking of trying Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) but not sure what to expect?
Whether you're exploring TCM for general wellness or seeking advice about a particular health concern, visiting a TCM clinic for the first time can raise plenty of questions.
What happens during a consultation? Will you need acupuncture? How do you know whether a practitioner is qualified?
Here's what to know before your first TCM visit in Singapore.
blog.content.tcm-singapore-first-visit.s: 1. What Is Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM)?
Traditional Chinese Medicine, commonly known as TCM, is a healthcare system with a long history rooted in Chinese medical traditions.

In Singapore, TCM practitioners may provide services such as consultations, acupuncture, herbal medicine and other traditional treatment approaches, depending on their qualifications and scope of practice.

TCM approaches health differently from conventional Western medicine. Its traditional concepts and diagnostic methods should not be assumed to have the same scientific basis as modern medical assessments.
The effectiveness and risks of specific TCM treatments vary, so it's important to understand what is being recommended before proceeding.
2. What Happens During Your First TCM Consultation?
Your first visit will typically begin with a discussion about your health concerns.
A TCM practitioner may ask about your symptoms, medical history, lifestyle, sleep, appetite and other aspects of your wellbeing.
Depending on the practitioner and your concerns, the consultation may also include traditional assessment methods such as observing your tongue or checking your pulse.
These are part of traditional TCM practice and should not be treated as substitutes for medically indicated diagnostic tests.
Tip: Bring along a list of medications, supplements and existing medical conditions so the practitioner can consider potential safety concerns.
3. Does Every TCM Visit Involve Acupuncture?
Not necessarily.
TCM clinics may offer different treatment approaches, including:
Acupuncture
The insertion of fine needles at selected points on the body.
Chinese herbal medicine
Traditional herbal preparations prescribed according to the practitioner's assessment.
Tui Na
A form of traditional Chinese therapeutic massage.
Cupping
A technique that uses suction cups on the skin.
Not every clinic provides every treatment, and not every treatment is appropriate for every patient.
Some treatments may cause side effects or interact with existing medications. Discuss the potential benefits, limitations and risks before starting.
4. How Do You Check Whether a TCM Practitioner Is Registered in Singapore?
In Singapore, TCM practitioners are regulated under the Traditional Chinese Medicine Practitioners Act.
Before your visit, you can check a practitioner's registration through the official TCM Practitioners Board.
Registration is an important consideration, but it does not guarantee a particular treatment outcome.
You should also feel comfortable asking about the practitioner's experience, proposed treatment and whether another form of medical assessment may be more appropriate.
5. How Much Does a TCM Consultation Cost?
TCM fees can vary depending on the clinic, practitioner and services provided.
A consultation fee may not include additional treatments or prescribed herbal medicines.
Before your visit, consider checking:
The initial consultation fee
Additional treatment charges
Costs of prescribed herbal medicine
Whether follow-up visits are recommended
Available payment methods and applicable benefits
Understanding the fees beforehand can help you plan your visit and avoid unexpected expenses.
6. Can You Visit a TCM Clinic Without an Appointment?
That depends on the clinic.
Some TCM providers may accept walk-ins, while others operate through scheduled appointments.
Before heading down, check the clinic's operating hours, appointment requirements and available services.
If you're visiting for the first time, you may also want to ask how much time to allow for your consultation.
Planning ahead can make the experience more convenient.
7. Choosing a TCM Clinic in Singapore
The right TCM clinic isn't necessarily the closest or most heavily advertised.
Consider whether the clinic provides clear information about its practitioners, services, fees and appointment arrangements.
A responsible practitioner should explain the proposed treatment, discuss relevant risks and recognise when conventional medical assessment or referral is needed.
Be cautious of guaranteed cures or claims that a treatment can replace necessary medical care.
If you have persistent, worsening or unexplained symptoms, seek appropriate medical evaluation rather than delaying diagnosis.

Trying a new healthcare service doesn't have to be confusing.
Take time to understand the practitioner's qualifications, the treatments offered, their potential risks and the expected costs.
Whether you're considering TCM for the first time or looking for a different provider, making an informed choice is more important than following trends or promotional claims.

blog.eyecare.body.0: LASIK, SMILE Pro, TransPRK or ICL? How I Help Patients Choose, as an Eye Surgeon Who Has Had Laser Vision Correction Myself
blog.eyecare.body.1: By Dr Philemon Huang, MBBS (S’pore), MMed (Ophth), FAMS, FRCOphth | Senior Consultant Ophthalmologist
blog.eyecare.body.2: Like many of my patients, I lived most of my life with myopia.
blog.eyecare.body.3: In 2021, I had TransPRK myself. It let me experience the procedure and the recovery through the eyes of a patient, not just the surgeon. My recovery went smoothly. I was able to let go of the daily reliance on spectacles, and rediscover the simple joy of waking up each morning to clear, natural eyesight.
blog.eyecare.body.4: So when patients sit down in my clinic and ask, “Doctor, which one is the best?”, I understand the question very well.
blog.eyecare.body.5: Here is my honest answer. There is no single best procedure. There is only the one that suits
blog.eyecare.body.8: Two patients of mine show why.
blog.eyecare.body.9: The first was a 38-year-old woman with high myopia and astigmatism, roughly -7 to -9 with about -3.5 of astigmatism. Correcting that much means removing more corneal tissue, and her corneas simply didn't have enough for SMILE Pro. We discussed ICL. She didn't like the idea of a procedure inside the eye, and the cost was higher than she wanted. So she went with TransPRK combined with corneal cross-linking (CXL) in both eyes. By about three weeks she was seeing 6/6 in both eyes, with no haze.
blog.eyecare.body.10: The second was a 29-year-old man, about -5.50 to -6.00. His priority was different. He had a wedding fair the very next day and needed to be functional quickly. His measurements suited SMILE Pro, so that is what he had, the day after his assessment. The morning after, he was seeing 6/7.5, close to normal, and 6/6 by day six.
blog.eyecare.body.11: Two different people, two different procedures, and both were the right choice for them. (Results vary from person to person, and these are not a promise for your eyes.)
blog.eyecare.body.12: First, what each option actually does
blog.eyecare.body.13: All four procedures aim for the same thing: getting light to focus properly on the retina so you can see clearly without glasses. They just work in different places.
blog.eyecare.body.15: A thin flap is created on the front of the cornea and lifted. A laser reshapes the tissue underneath, and the flap is put back. Visual recovery is usually very quick.
blog.eyecare.body.17: There is no flap. A laser shapes a thin disc of tissue (a “lenticule”) inside the cornea, and the surgeon removes it through a small keyhole opening. Studies have shown that the smaller opening helps preserve more corneal nerves, with a lower risk of dry eyes.
blog.eyecare.body.19: This is a surface treatment, and it’s the one I had. The laser works on the surface of the cornea in a single no-touch step, with no flap and no cut. Because the surface skin of the cornea needs to grow back, the first few days of recovery are generally slower and more uncomfortable than with LASIK or SMILE Pro.
blog.eyecare.body.21: This one doesn’t reshape the cornea at all. A thin lens is placed inside the eye, in front of your natural lens. It’s often considered for higher prescriptions, or when the cornea is too thin for laser treatment. Because it is surgery inside the eye, it comes with its own risks and needs long-term follow-up.
blog.eyecare.body.22: Think of it like getting a suit altered. LASIK and SMILE Pro take it in from the inside seams, TransPRK works on the outer fabric, and ICL leaves the suit alone and adds a well-fitted lining. All of them can give you a good fit. But which one a tailor chooses depends on the cloth he has to work with.
blog.eyecare.body.23: What really decides it: your eyes, not the brochure
blog.eyecare.body.24: I want to bring your attention to one thing. The decision is mostly made by measurements, not by preference.
blog.eyecare.body.25: At a proper suitability assessment, we look at:
blog.eyecare.body.27: How much myopia, astigmatism or long-sightedness there is, and whether it has been stable.
blog.eyecare.body.29: Laser procedures remove a small amount of corneal tissue. If the cornea is thin or has an irregular shape, some options become unsafe, and a lens-based option like ICL may be considered instead.
blog.eyecare.body.30: Your tear film and dry eye.
blog.eyecare.body.31: Dry eye before surgery tends to matter after surgery. This can tilt the decision towards a flapless option.
blog.eyecare.body.33: If you play contact sports such as soccer, rugby or martial arts, or in dynamic jobs such as the military, may find surface treatments like TransPRK more suitable because there is no flap to be dislodged.
blog.eyecare.body.35: From around 40, reading vision starts to change (presbyopia, or “lao hua”). Correcting your distance vision won’t stop that. It’s worth discussing before surgery, not after.
blog.eyecare.body.36: The health of the rest of your eye
blog.eyecare.body.37: , including your retina and your optic nerve.
blog.eyecare.body.38: That last point is close to my heart. My training is in glaucoma as well as refractive surgery, so I pay close attention to the optic nerve before any vision correction. Myopia is itself a risk factor for glaucoma. The Glaucoma Research Foundation also points out that eye pressure readings tend to read lower after laser vision correction, because the cornea is thinner. So the time to get a clean baseline of your eye pressure and optic nerve is
blog.eyecare.body.40: surgery. (I’ve written more about this in a separate article on what laser vision correction does and doesn’t change.)
blog.eyecare.body.41: “My friend did SMILE, so I’ll do SMILE”
blog.eyecare.body.42: You might be thinking this. Many people do.
blog.eyecare.body.43: Your friend’s eyes were measured, and the result suited your friend. Your cornea might be thicker or thinner. Your prescription might be higher. Your friend might play badminton on weekends while you play rugby, or the other way round. Choosing a procedure because it worked for someone else is a bit like borrowing their spectacles. They are excellent spectacles. Just not for you.
blog.eyecare.body.44: The same goes for online reviews and price comparisons. They tell you what someone else experienced. They can’t tell you what your corneal scan shows.
blog.eyecare.body.46: People often ask me whether there’s a “right age” for laser vision correction. There isn’t a perfect one, but there are a few principles.
blog.eyecare.body.47: Your prescription should be stable. If your myopia has still been creeping up over the past year or so, it’s usually wiser to wait, otherwise you could be correcting a moving target. That’s why most clinics look for adult patients whose prescription has settled.
blog.eyecare.body.48: At the other end, if you’re in your 40s, presbyopia is already on its way, and your plan should take that into account. Some people in this age group are better served by a different approach altogether, and a good surgeon will raise this with you rather than wait for you to discover it.
blog.eyecare.body.49: And if you’re planning a pregnancy, or you’re pregnant or breastfeeding, mention it. Hormonal changes can affect your prescription and your tear film, so timing may need to shift.
blog.eyecare.body.50: A quick comparison, in plain words
blog.eyecare.body.59: Cornea suitable, no strong reason to avoid a flap
blog.eyecare.body.61: Removes a lenticule through a keyhole
blog.eyecare.body.64: Myopia with or without astigmatism, dry eye concerns, contact sports
blog.eyecare.body.68: Slower and more uncomfortable for the first few days
blog.eyecare.body.69: Thinner corneas, contact sports or uniformed jobs, preference for no cut
blog.eyecare.body.71: Places a lens inside the eye
blog.eyecare.body.74: Higher prescriptions, thin corneas, not suitable for laser
blog.eyecare.body.75: This is a general guide only. Exact suitability ranges differ between machines and clinics, and your surgeon should explain the ones that apply to you.
blog.eyecare.body.77: I would not be doing my job if I only talked about the upside.
blog.eyecare.body.78: Laser procedures can cause dry eyes, glare or halos, especially in the early months. These usually settle, but not always completely. Surface treatments like TransPRK involve a few more days of discomfort at the start. LASIK carries flap-related risks, which are uncommon. ICL is surgery inside the eye, so it needs suitable internal measurements and regular check-ups afterwards.
blog.eyecare.body.79: And sometimes the right answer is no surgery at all. If your prescription is still changing, your cornea isn’t suitable, or there’s an eye condition that needs treating first, a good assessment should tell you so. That isn’t a failed consultation. It’s a successful one.
blog.eyecare.body.80: Sometimes the assessment finds something else entirely. I once saw a 31-year-old man who came in for a routine laser vision correction assessment and turned out to have glaucoma. He had no idea.
blog.eyecare.body.81: Questions to ask at your assessment
blog.eyecare.body.82: Write these down and bring them along:
blog.eyecare.body.83: Which procedures am I suitable for, and which am I
blog.eyecare.body.86: What did my corneal thickness and shape scans show?
blog.eyecare.body.87: Do I have any dry eye, and how will that be managed?
blog.eyecare.body.88: Has my optic nerve been checked, and what is my baseline eye pressure?
blog.eyecare.body.89: How will my reading vision change after 40, and does that affect my choice now?
blog.eyecare.body.90: What does recovery look like for my job and my sports?
blog.eyecare.body.91: What follow-up will I need, and for how long?
blog.eyecare.body.92: If your questions are answered clearly, without pressure, you’re in good hands. If you feel rushed, it’s perfectly fine to get a second opinion.
blog.eyecare.body.94: You don’t need to decide on a procedure today. Start with the assessment.
blog.eyecare.body.95: If you wear contact lenses, ask the clinic how long to stop wearing them before your appointment, because contact lenses can temporarily change the shape of the cornea and affect the measurements. Bring your current glasses and any old prescriptions you have.
blog.eyecare.body.96: To compare the different options in more detail, ask about
blog.eyecare.body.97: the laser vision correction options we offer at OneVision
blog.eyecare.body.99: ICL for higher prescriptions or thinner corneas
blog.eyecare.body.101: Having been on both sides of the laser, my advice is simple. Don’t ask which procedure is the best. Ask which one is right for your eyes, and why.
blog.eyecare.body.103: Dr Philemon Huang is a Senior Consultant Ophthalmologist and Medical Director of
blog.eyecare.body.105: at Mount Elizabeth Medical Centre, Singapore. He holds MBBS (S’pore), MMed (Ophth), FAMS and FRCOphth, and completed a glaucoma fellowship at Sydney Eye Hospital and Westmead Hospital, Australia, under a Ministry of Health HMDP award. He was previously Head of Glaucoma Services at Khoo Teck Puat Hospital. His practice covers refractive surgery (TransPRK, SMILE Pro, LASIK and ICL), cataract surgery and glaucoma care.
blog.eyecare.body.107:  Jiang X, Wang Y, Yuan H, et al. Influences of SMILE and FS-LASIK on Corneal Sub-basal Nerves: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis.
blog.eyecare.body.110:  Chen KY, Chan HC, Chan CM, et al. How Effective is Keratorefractive Lenticule Extraction Surgery (KLEx) in Reducing Dry Eye Outcomes Compared to LASIK? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
blog.eyecare.body.113:  Ahluwalia A, Manche EE. Comparing femtosecond LASIK and small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE).
blog.eyecare.body.116: This article is for general education and does not replace an individual consultation, examination or diagnosis by a qualified ophthalmologist. Suitability for any procedure can only be determined after a full eye assessment.
blog.eyecare.body.117: LASIK Corrected My Vision. Are My Eyes “Fixed” Now? 5 Myths a Glaucoma Specialist Hears After Laser Vision Correction
blog.eyecare.body.118: By Dr Philemon Huang, MBBS (S’pore), MMed (Ophth), FAMS, FRCOphth | Senior Consultant Ophthalmologist
blog.eyecare.body.119: If laser surgery fixed my eyes, why would I still need eye checks?
blog.eyecare.body.120: It’s a fair question. And it’s one I have a personal interest in, because I’m in the same group. I was myopic for most of my life and had TransPRK in 2021. It ended my daily reliance on spectacles. But my eyes are still the eyes of someone who grew up myopic.
blog.eyecare.body.121: I work in two sub-specialties that don’t always talk to each other: refractive surgery and glaucoma. Sitting between the two, I see where the gaps are. So allow me to go through five common beliefs about life after laser vision correction (LASIK, SMILE, PRK or TransPRK), and what the evidence actually says.
blog.eyecare.body.122: Let me tell you about one patient.
blog.eyecare.body.123: He was a man in his late twenties with very high myopia, and he had TransPRK. His prescription was corrected. But highly myopic eyes are predisposed to other conditions, glaucoma among them. Around two years later he had glaucoma, worse in his left eye. He needed laser treatment (SLT) and then glaucoma surgery (a trabeculectomy) in the left eye to bring it under control.
blog.eyecare.body.124: Today his pressures are controlled, and we keep watch over his remaining vision with regular visual field tests.
blog.eyecare.body.125: What I would like to highlight is this. The laser fixed his prescription. It did not fix the long, myopic eye underneath. That is why eye pressure and optic nerve checks still matter after laser.
blog.eyecare.body.130: Most myopia happens because the eyeball has grown too long, so light focuses in front of the retina instead of on it. Laser vision correction reshapes the front of the cornea so that light lands in the right place again. The length of the eyeball stays the same.
blog.eyecare.body.131: Here is a simple way to picture it. If your car’s headlights are angled wrongly, you can adjust them and see the road clearly again. But the car is still the same model, with the same engine and the same wear and tear. The adjustment changed where the light falls. It didn’t make the car new.
blog.eyecare.body.132: This matters because a long, myopic eye carries its own long-term risks, especially at higher prescriptions. These include retinal tears and detachment, myopic macular degeneration, and glaucoma. When a parent asked whether laser eye surgery would lower his highly myopic son’s risk of retinal detachment, the American Academy of Ophthalmology’s answer was no: removing the short-sightedness “will not make the eye anatomically different”. The eye is still long.
blog.eyecare.body.133: In Singapore this is not a small group. Data from the Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Diseases (SEED) study, reported in
blog.eyecare.body.135: in March 2026, found that about 6% of adults aged 40 to 80 had high myopia, and that around 30% of those with high myopia had myopic macular degeneration.
blog.eyecare.body.136: So keep watching for the warning signs of a retinal problem: a sudden shower of new floaters, flashes of light, or a shadow or curtain across part of your vision. These need to be seen urgently, the same day if possible.
blog.eyecare.body.137: the warning signs of a retinal tear
blog.eyecare.body.139: Myth 2: “My eye pressure reading is normal, so I don’t have glaucoma”
blog.eyecare.body.140: This one is close to my heart, because it can quietly mislead both patients and doctors.
blog.eyecare.body.141: Most eye pressure tests work by pressing on, or puffing air at, the cornea. Laser vision correction makes the cornea thinner and changes how it flexes. The result is that the pressure reading often comes out
blog.eyecare.body.144: How much lower? A systematic review and meta-analysis published in the
blog.eyecare.body.146: in 2026 pooled 54 studies covering 4,730 eyes. With the standard Goldmann method, measured eye pressure after LASIK was on average about 3 mmHg lower than before surgery, and about 2 mmHg lower after PRK. Newer devices were affected less, but none removed the effect entirely.
blog.eyecare.body.147: Three millimetres of mercury sounds tiny. In glaucoma care, it can be the difference between “normal” and “needs a closer look”.
blog.eyecare.body.148: I want to bring your attention to the practical lesson here. After laser vision correction, a single pressure number should never be the only test. A proper glaucoma assessment looks at the optic nerve itself, with an OCT scan of the nerve fibre layer and a visual field test, and takes your corneal thickness into account. If you have had laser vision correction,
blog.eyecare.body.149: always tell whoever is measuring your eye pressure
blog.eyecare.body.150: , including at an optician or a health screening.
blog.eyecare.body.151: The Glaucoma Research Foundation adds another reason. The steroid eye drops commonly used after laser vision correction can raise eye pressure in some people, and the falsely low readings can mask that rise. That’s why post-operative checks matter, and why stopping your drops early or extending them on your own is not a good idea.
blog.eyecare.body.154: reported SNEC data showing that glaucoma operations for patients aged 40 to 49 nearly tripled, from 22 in 2015 to 60 in 2025, with untreated myopia in earlier generations suggested as a likely factor, alongside better access to screening. Glaucoma is no longer only a condition of the elderly.
blog.eyecare.body.155: For information on a full eye assessment, see
blog.eyecare.body.156: how glaucoma is assessed and managed
blog.eyecare.body.159: For distance, hopefully not for a long time. For reading, almost certainly yes.
blog.eyecare.body.160: From around 40, the natural lens inside the eye gradually loses its flexibility. This is presbyopia, the “lao hua” that has you holding your phone further and further away. Laser vision correction on the cornea doesn’t stop the lens from ageing.
blog.eyecare.body.161: I say this not to spoil anyone’s celebration. I say it so that nobody feels their surgery has “failed” at 45. It hasn’t. Your eyes are simply turning 45 too. Surgeons’ eyes included.
blog.eyecare.body.162: If you are approaching 40 and considering laser vision correction, ask your surgeon how presbyopia will affect you later. There are options, and planning ahead helps.
blog.eyecare.body.163: Myth 4: “If I need cataract surgery one day, it will be the same as anyone else’s”
blog.eyecare.body.164: Not quite. And this one depends on paperwork you may not have thought about.
blog.eyecare.body.165: During cataract surgery, the cloudy natural lens is replaced with an artificial lens. The surgeon calculates the power of that lens using measurements of your cornea. After laser vision correction, the cornea’s shape has changed, and standard calculations become less accurate. The American Academy of Ophthalmology notes that refractive outcomes of cataract surgery are less precise in eyes that have had previous excimer laser surgery for myopia, and that patients should be told about this limitation.
blog.eyecare.body.166: There is something simple you can do. Ask for, and keep, a copy of your refractive surgery records: your prescription and corneal measurements before surgery, and your stable prescription a few months after. The Academy has encouraged surgeons to give patients a card with these values for exactly this reason. File it with your important documents. Your future cataract surgeon will thank you.
blog.eyecare.body.167: And when that day comes, tell them you’ve had laser vision correction, even if it was twenty years ago.
blog.eyecare.body.168: Myth 5: “If I had glaucoma, I could never have had laser vision correction”
blog.eyecare.body.169: You might have heard this, and it’s not quite right either.
blog.eyecare.body.170: The American Academy of Ophthalmology states that glaucoma is not, by itself, a reason to rule out LASIK. What matters is how severe the glaucoma is, how healthy the optic nerve looks on visual field and OCT testing, and whether the eye pressure is well controlled. In some patients with glaucoma, a surface treatment or a flapless procedure may be preferred, because creating a LASIK flap briefly raises the pressure inside the eye.
blog.eyecare.body.171: The flip side is just as important. If you are a glaucoma suspect, have a family history of glaucoma, or are on glaucoma drops, your refractive surgeon needs to know. The planning, the choice of procedure and the follow-up may all change.
blog.eyecare.body.172: So what should you actually do?
blog.eyecare.body.173: If you have had laser vision correction, here is a simple plan:
blog.eyecare.body.175: that looks at your optic nerve and retina, not just your vision. If you haven’t had one since your surgery, start there.
blog.eyecare.body.177: that you’ve had laser vision correction, especially when your eye pressure is being measured.
blog.eyecare.body.179: , ideally your pre-operative prescription and corneal measurements.
blog.eyecare.body.181: : sudden floaters, flashes, a curtain over your vision, or sudden eye pain with blurred vision. These need same-day attention.
blog.eyecare.body.183: If a parent or sibling has glaucoma, you are at higher risk.
blog.eyecare.body.186: How often you need checks after that depends on your age, prescription and risk factors, so let your eye doctor set the interval.
blog.eyecare.body.187: Laser vision correction made a real difference to my daily life. But it corrected my focus. It didn’t change the eye underneath. So enjoy your clear vision, and keep your eyes checked.

blog.eyecare.body.204: Turning 40 in Singapore? The Eye Check I Recommend, and Why
blog.eyecare.body.205: By Dr Philemon Huang, MBBS (S’pore), MMed (Ophth), FAMS, FRCOphth | Senior Consultant Ophthalmologist
blog.eyecare.body.206: Try this. Pick up your phone and read a message at your usual distance.
blog.eyecare.body.207: Did you push it a little further away? Did you take off your glasses to read it? Did you blame the font?
blog.eyecare.body.208: If so, welcome. You may have met “lao hua”. Singapore General Hospital describes presbyopia as a condition that usually starts around the age of 40, and the classic sign is exactly that: holding your phone further away to read it.
blog.eyecare.body.209: 老花眼 “Lao hua” itself is not dangerous. It’s simply the lens inside your eye becoming less flexible with age, and it’s easily helped. But I want to use it as a reminder. Because 40 is also the age when the eye conditions that
blog.eyecare.body.211: announce themselves start becoming more common. And those are the ones I’d rather catch early.
blog.eyecare.body.212: One patient comes to mind, and he wasn't even 40.
blog.eyecare.body.213: He was a 31-year-old man who came in for a routine laser vision correction assessment. As part of the assessment we examined his optic nerves, and found glaucoma, with a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.8 in both eyes. He had no idea. He is now on eye drops, and his serial visual field tests have stayed stable.
blog.eyecare.body.214: Early-onset eye problems can happen to anyone. A thorough assessment checks more than your prescription. And if it can turn up glaucoma at 31, it is certainly worth doing at 40.
blog.eyecare.body.216: The American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends that adults with no signs or risk factors for eye disease get a baseline eye examination at 40. That’s the age when early signs of disease and changes in vision may start to appear.
blog.eyecare.body.217: The word “baseline” matters. A baseline is a set of measurements of
blog.eyecare.body.219: eyes when they are healthy, or close to it. Later, any change can be compared against it. It’s a bit like having a photo of your car the day you collect it. If a scratch appears two years later, you know it’s new.
blog.eyecare.body.220: Singapore gives us a few more reasons to take this seriously.
blog.eyecare.body.221: We are a very myopic population.
blog.eyecare.body.222: The Singapore Epidemiology of Eye Diseases (SEED) study found that about 36% of adults aged 40 to 80 had myopia and about 6% had high myopia, as reported in
blog.eyecare.body.224: in March 2026. Myopia, especially high myopia, raises the long-term risk of glaucoma, retinal detachment and myopic macular degeneration.
blog.eyecare.body.226: The same report cited Singapore National Eye Centre data showing that glaucoma operations for patients aged 40 to 49 nearly tripled, from 22 in 2015 to 60 in 2025. Untreated myopia in earlier generations was suggested as a likely factor, along with better access to screening.
blog.eyecare.body.227: The condition I worry about most at this age
blog.eyecare.body.228: You’ll forgive me for being biased. My sub-specialty is glaucoma.
blog.eyecare.body.229: Glaucoma damages the optic nerve, the cable that carries information from the eye to the brain. In most types, it does this slowly and painlessly. It usually takes away side vision first, while your central vision stays sharp. So you can read the eye chart perfectly well and still have glaucoma.
blog.eyecare.body.230: Here is the hard part. The vision lost to glaucoma cannot be brought back. Treatment aims to stop or slow further damage. That’s why it is called the silent thief of sight, and why finding it early makes such a difference.
blog.eyecare.body.231: how glaucoma steals vision quietly, and how it is managed
blog.eyecare.body.233: You might be thinking: “But my eyes feel fine.” That is exactly the point. With early glaucoma, they usually do.
blog.eyecare.body.234: What a proper 40s eye check should include
blog.eyecare.body.235: A quick vision test at an optical shop is useful for updating your spectacles. It’s not the same as a medical eye examination. At 40, I’d look for these:
blog.eyecare.body.237: Your distance and near vision, and whether lao hua has started.
blog.eyecare.body.239: Raised pressure is a major risk factor for glaucoma. It’s only one piece of the puzzle, though. Many people with glaucoma have normal pressure readings.
blog.eyecare.body.240: A look at the optic nerve.
blog.eyecare.body.241: This is the key one for glaucoma. If there is any doubt, an OCT scan (a quick, painless scan of the nerve fibre layer) and a visual field test can give more detail.
blog.eyecare.body.243: Especially if you are myopic. We check for thinning areas or tears at the edges of the retina, and for changes at the macula, the centre of your vision.
blog.eyecare.body.245: Early cataract changes, dry eye, and whether the drainage angle of the eye is open or narrow.
blog.eyecare.body.246: Your eye doctor may dilate your pupils with drops to see the retina properly. If so, your vision will be blurry and light-sensitive for a few hours. Bring sunglasses, and please don’t drive yourself home.
blog.eyecare.body.247: “But I already do a health screening every year”
blog.eyecare.body.248: Good. Please keep doing it. Company and government health screenings are useful, and as the Straits Times report pointed out, better access to screening may be one reason glaucoma is being picked up earlier in Singapore.
blog.eyecare.body.249: But a screening is a quick sieve. It’s designed to catch the obvious things in a large number of people in a short time. A comprehensive eye examination is slower. It looks at the whole eye, compares both sides, and lets someone trained in eye disease look directly at your optic nerve and retina.
blog.eyecare.body.250: The same goes for a spectacle check at the optical shop. Your optometrist can pick up a lot, and will often refer you on if something looks unusual. Still, a new pair of glasses that makes the eye chart sharp doesn’t tell you much about your optic nerve.
blog.eyecare.body.251: Think of it as the difference between a quick car wash and a full servicing. Both have their place. Only one looks under the bonnet.
blog.eyecare.body.253: The baseline at 40 is for people with no risk factors. Some of you should be seen earlier, or more often:
blog.eyecare.body.255: If a parent, brother or sister has glaucoma, your own risk is higher.
blog.eyecare.body.256: why glaucoma might runs in families
blog.eyecare.body.259: Particularly if you’ve worn thick lenses since school, even if you’ve since had laser vision correction.
blog.eyecare.body.261: Diabetes can damage the blood vessels of the retina. People with diabetes should have their eyes screened regularly, usually every year.
blog.eyecare.body.263: , including steroid eye drops, inhalers or tablets, which can raise eye pressure in some people.
blog.eyecare.body.266: That depends on what the baseline shows. For adults without risk factors, the American Academy of Ophthalmology suggests a check every two to four years between 40 and 54, and every one to three years between 55 and 64. If you have risk factors, or something needs watching, your eye doctor will set a shorter interval.
blog.eyecare.body.267: Don’t wait for your next check if you notice these
blog.eyecare.body.268: Some symptoms need attention within the day, not at your next routine appointment:
blog.eyecare.body.269: Sudden blurring or loss of vision in one eye
blog.eyecare.body.270: A sudden shower of new floaters, or flashes of light
blog.eyecare.body.271: A shadow or curtain coming across part of your vision
blog.eyecare.body.272: A red, painful eye with blurred vision, especially with headache, nausea or vomiting, or seeing haloes around lights
blog.eyecare.body.273: The last one can be a sign of acute angle-closure glaucoma, which is an emergency. Go to an eye doctor or the emergency department straight away.
blog.eyecare.body.274: A small step for your 40th year
blog.eyecare.body.275: Here is my suggestion. Don’t treat it as another chore. Treat it as a birthday present to your future self.
blog.eyecare.body.276: Book one proper eye examination this year. Before you go, ask your parents and siblings whether anyone has glaucoma, and bring your current glasses or your last prescription. If you’ve had laser vision correction, bring whatever records you have.
blog.eyecare.body.277: And if you’ve found yourself holding the menu at arm’s length at your birthday dinner, you’ll have something to ask about too.
blog.eyecare.body.280: Forty is a good age. Let’s keep your eyes good for the next forty years too.
